item.title: 1.1 Why Spiking Neural Networks Exist
item.description: Why Spiking Neural Networks Exist Imagine a small sensor watching a doorway.

item.title: 1.2 Spikes, Timing, and Event-Driven Computation
item.description: Spikes, Timing, and Event-Driven Computation A neuron activation gives a network a value to pass forward, and a simulation timestep provides a moment at which the network can update that value.

item.title: 1.3 The Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neuron
item.description: The Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Neuron A spike event happens at a particular time, but a neuron needs a way to decide when that event should occur.

item.title: 1.4 From Encoded Input to Spike Trains
item.description: From Encoded Input to Spike Trains A leaky integrate-and-fire neuron already gives us a way to turn incoming events into an outgoing spike: it accumulates their effects over time, leaks some accumulated state away, and fires when its threshold is reached.

item.title: 1.5 Winner-Take-All Competition
item.description: Winner-Take-All Competition A spike train can carry several possible interpretations into a layer of excitatory neurons.

item.title: 2.1 How SNNs Learn
item.description: How SNNs Learn Once a spiking neuron has integrated its inputs and emitted a spike, the network still faces the familiar training problem: its connections must change so that future outputs better match the desired behavior.
